No power: check the battery and terminals
If the dashboard is completely dark, current from the battery isn’t reaching the car. Most often the terminals or a completely flat battery are to blame.
Open the hood and wiggle the battery terminals by hand. They shouldn’t be loose.
If there is white or green deposit on the terminals, remove them (negative first, then positive), clean them and put them back (positive first, then negative).
Switch on the headlights. If they don’t light or are very dim, the battery is flat: jump-start from another car or charge it.
Check the main power fuse (below).
Check the battery isolator switch — by the batteries or a button in the cab. It must be switched on.
In a 24 V system two batteries are connected by a jumper cable. Check that it is intact and tight.
The battery is most likely flat
The starter doesn’t get enough current: it cranks sluggishly and the lights dim. This happens especially often in frost and with batteries older than 4–5 years.
Check the terminals: are they tight, is there any deposit?
Jump-start from another car. Red cable: your battery positive → donor positive. Black: donor negative → bare metal on your car’s engine.
Let the donor run for 5–10 minutes, then start. Crank for no longer than 10 seconds and wait 30 seconds between attempts.
If the battery goes flat overnight again, there is a current drain or the alternator isn’t charging.
Only jump-start a 24 V vehicle from a 24 V vehicle or a 24 V jump starter.
Two batteries work as a pair: if one is weak, it drags both down. Measure each one — a good one shows 12.4–12.9 V.
There’s a click, but the starter doesn’t crank
A click means the starter solenoid has engaged and the start command is getting through. Either there isn’t enough current or the starter itself is jammed.
Switch on the headlights and turn the key again. If the headlights dim a lot, the problem is the battery or terminals.
Check that the thick cable on the starter and the ground strap from the engine to the body (frame) are tight.
Try the method from the tip below.

Tap the starter housing a few times with a hammer or a tyre iron — not hard, but firmly. Then try to start. If that doesn’t help, have a helper hold the key on “Start” while you tap. If it starts, the starter is worn — repair it before it fails completely.
The starter is silent: check the lockout and the fuse
Complete silence means the start command doesn’t reach the starter. Often this is the in-gear start protection or a blown fuse.
Automatic: is the lever definitely in P? Shift to N and try again.
Manual: press the clutch all the way down. Many cars won’t start without it.
Start button: press it with the brake pedal pressed.
Check the starter fuse and relay (below). You can temporarily swap the relay with a neighbouring one with the same marking.
If a key or lock symbol is flashing, the immobilizer may be blocking the start.
Check the battery isolator switch.
On some trucks the starter won’t engage if the cab isn’t locked down after tilting.
Checked everything and the starter is still silent? Tap its housing with a hammer and try again. Sometimes the solenoid contacts get burnt, and a light tap helps you get to a workshop.
Looks like the fuel pump isn’t working
When the ignition is switched on, the pump hums for 2–3 seconds and builds pressure. If it’s silent, it isn’t getting power or it has seized.
Make sure there is fuel in the tank. If the tank is almost empty, add 5–10 litres.
Check the fuel pump fuse (below).
Find the pump relay and swap it with a neighbouring one with the same marking. If the pump starts humming, replace the relay.
On many trucks the fuel is fed by a mechanical pump on the high-pressure pump. Bleed the system with the hand primer pump until it becomes firm.

Have a helper switch on the ignition while you knock with your fist or a rubber mallet on the bottom of the tank. On many cars the pump sits under the rear seat: lift the seat, open the hatch and tap the pump cover. If the pump starts humming and the car starts, it is worn — replace it soon.
Don’t hit the tank with metal objects, don’t smoke and don’t use an open flame nearby.
The pump hums, but the engine won’t start
The pump is getting power. The cause may be fuel pressure, the filter, ignition or sensors, and it can’t be found without a scanner.
Check the ECU and ignition fuses (below).
If you filled up recently, you may have got poor-quality fuel.
Don’t crank the starter for longer than 10 seconds at a time, pause for 30 seconds so you don’t drain the battery.
Oleg will run a computer diagnosis on site and find the cause.
The immobilizer is blocking the start
A key or lock symbol means the car doesn’t recognise the key and won’t let it start. The engine may not start or may die after 1–2 seconds.
Try the spare key.
Replace the battery in the key fob.
Car with a Start button: hold the key fob right against the button and press it. On many cars there is an antenna there.
If you have an alarm with remote start, disarm the car again with the alarm fob.
Oleg repairs immobilizers.
Fuel is being supplied — a diagnosis is needed
The starter cranks, the pump works, the immobilizer isn’t interfering. The cause lies in the ignition, sensors or ECU, and only a scanner can show it.
See if Check Engine is on after a start attempt. If you have a scanner, read the codes and decode them on the “Error codes” tab.
If you filled up recently, you may have got poor-quality petrol.
Don’t crank the starter for longer than 10 seconds at a time, pause for 30 seconds.
Add fuel first
With an almost empty tank, especially on a slope, the pump may suck air. The fuel level sensor can also be wrong sometimes.
Add 5–10 litres.
Switch on the ignition for 3 seconds, switch it off and repeat 2–3 times — the pump will build up pressure.
After running out of fuel, a diesel must be bled with the hand primer pump.
If it still won’t start with fuel, tap “Back” and choose “Yes, there’s fuel”.
The electric car won’t switch on: check the 12 V battery
An electric car also has an ordinary 12 V battery. It powers the control units and switches on the high-voltage battery. If it is flat, the car won’t switch on even with a full traction battery.
Press the brake pedal and the Start button: READY should appear on the dashboard.
Replace the battery in the key fob or hold the fob to the backup start spot (see the owner’s manual).
Measure the 12 V battery voltage: below 12 V — charge it or connect a jump starter as described in the manual. Only connect to the 12 V system.
If the car won’t switch on with a charged 12 V battery, a diagnosis is needed.
Oleg will check the 12 V system and the control units with a scanner.
No power: battery, terminals or the main fuse
If the dash doesn’t light up at all, current from the battery isn’t reaching the motorcycle. Most often the battery is flat, the terminals have come loose or the main fuse has blown.
Remove the seat or side cover and check the battery terminals: the small bolts often work loose from vibration.
Measure the battery voltage: below 12 V, it needs charging.
Check the main fuse (below). It is often right on the starter relay, next to the battery.
Check the ignition switch and the connector under it: the dash should light up when you turn the key.

After winter a motorcycle battery is almost always flat. Charge it with a motorcycle battery charger at a low current — about a tenth of the capacity (for 8 Ah — about 0.8 A). Lithium batteries must only be charged with a charger that has a lithium mode.
A motorcycle battery is small and drains quickly: after winter, from an alarm, or if the bike has stood for a long time. The starter cranks sluggishly and the dash dims.
Measure the voltage: a charged battery shows 12.6–12.9 V (lithium — 13.0–13.4 V).
Charge the battery with a motorcycle battery charger.
You can jump-start from a car, but only with the car’s engine off: the car’s alternator can damage the motorcycle’s electronics.

With a manual gearbox you can bump-start it: 2nd gear, pull the clutch, push it up to speed and release the clutch sharply. On a fuel-injected bike this only works if the battery isn’t completely flat.
If the battery goes flat again within a couple of days, check the charging (“Sensors” tab, 5000 rpm mode).
The relay clicks, but the starter doesn’t crank
A click means the starter relay engages, but current doesn’t reach the starter. Most often it’s a weak battery, corroded terminals or burnt relay contacts.
Check and tighten the battery terminals and the thick cable on the starter.
Check the ground: the cable from the battery to the frame or engine.
Measure the voltage while pressing the starter: below 9.6 V — the battery can’t cope.
Tap the starter housing a few times with a hammer handle or a tyre iron and try again. If it starts, the starter is worn (brushes or bushings) — get it repaired.
Motorcycle in neutral and on its stand. Keep your hands away from the chain and the wheel.
The starter is silent: check the safety cut-offs
Motorcycles and scooters have many protections against accidental starting. The starter is almost always silent because of one of them, not because of a breakdown.
The engine stop switch (Run/Stop, usually red on the right handlebar) is on RUN.
Neutral: the green N light is on. Or pull the clutch all the way in.
Side stand: on many motorcycles the starter won’t engage or the engine dies if the side stand is down and a gear is engaged. Raise it.
Scooter: the starter only works with the brake held.
Check the main fuse and the starter relay (below).
The side stand sensor and the clutch switch often corrode or break. If the bike only starts in neutral or dies when you engage a gear, they are the problem.
Carburettor: check the fuel and the choke
The starter cranks but the engine won’t catch. On carburettor bikes it’s most often the fuel tap, the choke, stale petrol or a flooded spark plug.
Fuel tap on ON or RES (reserve). A vacuum tap has a PRI position — it lets fuel through without vacuum.
When cold, use the choke (CHOKE lever) and turn it off after starting.
If the bike stood all winter, the petrol may have gone stale. Drain the petrol from the float bowls via the screws at the bottom of the carburettor and fill with fresh petrol.
Unscrew the spark plug: if it’s wet and smells of petrol, it’s flooded. Dry it, crank the engine without the plug and screw it back in.
Check the spark (tip below).

Put the cap on the removed spark plug, press its thread against the engine metal and press the starter: there should be a bright blue spark. If it’s weak or absent — the plug, coil or ignition module.
Hold the spark plug with insulated pliers. There must be no spilled petrol nearby.
Looks like the fuel pump isn’t working
On a fuel-injected motorcycle the in-tank pump hums for 2–3 seconds and builds pressure when you switch on the ignition. If it’s silent, the pump isn’t getting power or it has seized.
Check the Run/Stop switch: in the STOP position the pump doesn’t switch on.
Check that there is petrol in the tank.
Check the injection and fuel pump fuse (below) and the pump relay.
Look at the pump connector on the tank: on motorcycles it often corrodes.
Switch on the ignition and tap the tank with your palm from below or from the side where the pump sits. If it starts humming, the pump is worn and needs replacing soon.
Don’t hit the tank with metal, don’t smoke nearby.
The pump works — check the spark and the error codes
Fuel is being supplied, but the engine won’t catch. The cause lies in the ignition, sensors or ECU.
Look at the dash: if the FI light is flashing or the engine symbol is on, the ECU has stored a fault. Count the flashes or read the code on the screen and enter it on the “Error codes” tab.
If the key symbol is flashing, the immobilizer may be blocking the start. Try the spare key.
Check the spark plugs and the spark.
Check the injection fuse (below).
Oleg will connect a scanner to the motorcycle and find the cause.
The battery keeps going flat: check the charging
The most common cause on motorcycles is a faulty regulator/rectifier or alternator stator. Less often a current drain (alarm, connected gadgets) or an old battery.
Start the engine and measure the battery voltage at 4000–5000 rpm with the headlight on. The norm is 13.5–14.8 V.
Below 13.5 V — not charging: the regulator/rectifier or the stator. Above 15 V — overcharging, the regulator/rectifier is faulty.
Inspect the connector between the stator and the regulator/rectifier: it often burns and melts.
If the battery is more than 3–4 years old, load-test it.
Oleg will check the stator and the regulator/rectifier and find the current drain.
Check the lights and turn signals
On a motorcycle almost all the lighting goes through the handlebar switches, and they corrode from moisture. Start with the simple things.
If one bulb doesn’t light, replace the bulb.
If nothing lights at all, check the lighting fuse (below).
If the turn signals flash very fast, a bulb has blown or LED indicators were fitted without an LED flasher relay.
If the turn signals don’t flash at all — the flasher relay. Fit an LED or a standard one, depending on your bulbs.
Flick the handlebar switches several times: if the light flickers, the contacts are corroded and need cleaning.
FI light on or an error on the dash

The motorcycle’s ECU has stored a fault. On new motorcycles (Euro 5) the codes are read with an OBD scanner, like on cars. Many Japanese motorcycles show the code as a number on the dash or by flashing the FI light.
If the code is shown as a number on the dash, write it down.
If the FI light is flashing, count the flashes: on Honda long flashes are tens, short ones are units.
Enter the code on the “Error codes” tab or take a photo of the dash.
If the light is flashing and the engine jerks or dies, don’t ride far.
Oleg will decode the code for your make and find the cause.
The engine is overheating: check the fan
On liquid-cooled motorcycles the fan switches on at about 100–105 °C. In traffic without the fan the engine overheats quickly.
Don’t open the radiator cap on a hot engine: steam and coolant will scald you.
Switch off the engine and let it cool down.
Check the coolant level in the expansion tank.
Check the fan fuse (below).
Look at the connectors of the fan and the temperature sensor.
Until it’s fixed, switch off the engine during long stops in traffic.
The electric motorcycle or scooter won’t move
Electric vehicles refuse to move because of safety cut-offs more often than because of breakdowns.
Don’t open the traction battery: high voltage and a fire risk.
Check the battery charge and that it is installed correctly and latched.
Side stand up, Run/Stop switch on RUN.
On many scooters you need to hold the brake and press a button to enter ride mode.
If the battery is completely flat, the protection may have switched it off. Charge it for a few hours with the original charger.
Look at the error code on the display and enter it on the “Error codes” tab.
Oleg will check the wiring, connectors and the control unit.
The glow plugs don’t work
A cold diesel needs glow plugs: they heat the combustion chambers before starting. If the coil symbol doesn’t come on or flashes, the plugs are most likely not heating.
Check the glow plug power fuse (below).
Find the glow plug relay or control unit and check its connector.
Check the plugs with a multimeter: a good one reads almost 0 Ω (usually under 2 Ω); an open circuit means the plug has burned out.
On many cars a flashing coil symbol means an engine fault — read the code with a scanner.
Many trucks have an intake air heater (flame or electric) instead of glow plugs. It has its own relay and power fuse.
Diesel in frost: check the fuel
Preheating works, but the engine won’t catch. In winter the cause is most often gelled summer fuel (wax) or frozen water in the filter.
Don’t heat the fuel filter, tank or lines with an open flame — that’s a fire.
Think about where you filled up. In winter you need winter or arctic diesel.
Put the vehicle in a warm garage for a few hours — the wax will melt.
Drain the water from the fuel filter/separator (the tap at the bottom of the filter).
Check the fuel filter heater (if fitted) and its fuse.
Crank the starter for no longer than 10–15 seconds, with pauses — save the battery.
Looks like there is air in the fuel system
After a filter change, running out of fuel or a long period standing, air gets into the fuel and the diesel won’t start.
Bleed the system with the hand primer pump (bulb or button on the filter) until it becomes firm.
On some vehicles you can switch on the ignition several times for 10–15 seconds — the electric lift pump will bleed the system by itself.
Check for fuel leaks at the filter and connections: air gets sucked in through them.
If it won’t start after bleeding, check the rail pressure while cranking (“Sensors” tab).
The diesel fuel system needs checking
The starter cranks, but the diesel won’t catch. The cause may be fuel pressure, injectors, sensors or the ECU.
Check that there is fuel and the filter isn’t clogged.
Drain the water from the fuel filter/separator.
If you have a scanner, check the rail pressure while cranking. Usually at least 200 bar is needed to start (“Sensors” tab).
Read the error codes and decode them on the “Error codes” tab.
Oleg will run a computer diagnosis of the diesel on site.
The engine has limited its power
A diesel goes into a power limit when it detects a fault in the AdBlue (SCR) system or the particulate filter, or a threat to the engine. The error code will show the exact cause.
Check the AdBlue level and top it up if it’s low. Only use AdBlue, never water.
AdBlue freezes at −11 °C in winter: after starting, wait for the tank heater to work.
Read the error code on the dashboard or with a scanner and decode it on the “Error codes” tab.
If the particulate filter symbol is on, drive steadily on the highway for 20–30 minutes. If that doesn’t help, a forced regeneration is needed.
Oleg will read the codes with a scanner and find the cause of the power limit.
The fan isn’t supposed to spin yet
The radiator fan only switches on when the engine has warmed up to about 95–105 °C. On a cold engine it stays still — this is normal.
Check again when the needle reaches the middle or slightly above.
If the needle rises above the middle and the fan still hasn’t switched on, go back and choose the second option.
Trucks often have a viscous-clutch fan: on a cold engine it turns slowly and easily, on a hot one it engages.
Check the radiator fan fuse
The fan doesn’t switch on from temperature or from the A/C. Most likely it isn’t getting power: a fuse, relay or connector.
Switch off the engine.
Swap the fan relay with a neighbouring one with the same marking.
Look at the connector on the fan motor: has it come loose, is there corrosion?
Until it’s fixed, watch the temperature needle. In traffic, turn the heater up to maximum: it will take away some of the heat.
If a viscous or electromagnetic clutch fan doesn’t spin on a hot engine, check the clutch and its connector (on the electromagnetic one).
The fan motor is fine, the control is failing
Since the fan spins with the A/C on, the motor, fuse and wiring are fine. It isn’t being switched on by temperature because of the sensor, relay or ECU.
Until it’s repaired you can drive with the A/C on — the fan will work.
Watch the temperature needle, especially in traffic jams.
Oleg will check the sensor and the fan control with a scanner.
Pull over and switch off the engine
The needle in the red zone means overheating. If you keep driving, the cylinder head may warp, and that is an expensive repair.
Don’t open the radiator or expansion tank cap on a hot engine: steam and coolant will scald you.
Stop in a safe place and switch off the engine.
Wait 30–40 minutes for the engine to cool down.
Check the coolant level in the tank. If it’s below the MIN mark, top up with coolant (in summer, water as a last resort).
Check the radiator fan fuse (below).
Don’t drive while overheating. Call Oleg out or call a tow truck.
Check the heater fuse
The heater fan is silent at all speeds. Most often the fuse has blown, the relay has failed or the motor has seized.
Turn the speed switch through all positions.
Check the heater fuse (below).
Swap the heater relay with a neighbouring one with the same marking.

The heater motor is usually under the glovebox on the passenger side. Turn the heater to maximum and tap its housing from below with your palm. If it starts spinning, the brushes or bearing are worn — the motor will need replacing soon.
The heater resistor has burned out
If the heater only blows on the highest speed, the fuse and motor are fine. Speeds 1–3 go through the resistor, and it has burned out.
Until it’s replaced, use the highest speed.
The resistor is inexpensive and usually sits next to the motor under the glovebox. Get one exactly for your model.
If a new resistor burns out quickly, the motor is binding and overloading it.
Blowing cold: the cooling system is the cause
The fan works, but the air doesn’t get warm. Most often it’s low coolant, an air lock, a thermostat that doesn’t close or a clogged heater core.
With the engine cold, check the coolant level in the expansion tank.
Look at the temperature needle. If it’s below the middle after 15 minutes of driving, it’s most likely the thermostat.
Set the control to maximum heat and listen under the dashboard. On cars with climate control the flap motor should operate.
If coolant keeps disappearing, look for a leak — it can damage the engine.
Oleg repairs heating systems.
Most likely a bulb has blown
When one headlight is out, the bulb is almost always to blame. On many cars each headlight also has its own fuse.
If the headlights are xenon, don’t take them apart yourself: the ballast produces high voltage.
Remove the bulb and look at it. A broken filament or a darkened glass means the bulb has blown.
To check, swap the bulbs of the left and right headlights.
Don’t touch the glass of a new halogen bulb with your fingers — the grease will make it burn out quickly.
If the new bulb doesn’t light either, check the fuse for this headlight (below).
In a 24 V system only fit 24 V bulbs — a 12 V bulb will blow immediately.
Check the headlight fuses and relay
Both bulbs rarely blow at the same time. Usually a fuse, a relay or the stalk switch is to blame.
Check both headlight fuses, left and right (below).
Swap the headlight relay with a neighbouring one with the same marking.
If low beam doesn’t work but high beam does (or vice versa), the stalk switch is often to blame.
Check the parking light fuse
Parking lights and tail lights are usually powered by one fuse. The instrument and button illumination often goes out with them.
Check the parking light fuse (below).
If one lamp is out, replace the bulb and check the socket for corrosion.
On a tractor unit, check the trailer socket and its connector: corroded contacts are a common cause.
The brake lights don’t work
When both brake lights are out, the fuse or the switch above the brake pedal is to blame.
Driving without brake lights is dangerous: drivers behind can’t see you braking.
Check the brake light fuse (below).
Look at the switch above the brake pedal: is the stop broken, has the connector come off?
On trucks with air brakes the brake lights are switched by a pressure switch — check it and its connector.
Check the power window fuse
All the motors rarely fail at once. Look for a common cause.
Check the window lock button on the driver’s door: is it pressed?
Check the power window fuse (below).
Swap the power window relay with a neighbouring one with the same marking.
One window doesn’t work
The fuse usually has nothing to do with it. The cause is the switch, the motor, the regulator or the wires in the boot between the door and the body.
Press the switch and listen. If the motor hums but the window doesn’t move, the cable or regulator is broken.
If there’s complete silence, try raising this window with the switch on the driver’s door. If it works from there, the switch on this door is broken.
While holding the switch, tap the door panel with your palm. If the window moves, the motor brushes are worn.
Open the door and look at the rubber boot with the wires: the wires often break there.
Check the central locking
First work out where the fault is: in the key fob or in the lock itself.
Lock with the button inside the cabin or with the key in the door. If that works, the problem is the key fob: replace its battery.
If nothing works, check the central locking fuse (below).
If one door doesn’t work, it’s most likely the lock actuator in that door or the wires in the boot.
Check the cigarette lighter fuse
This fuse blows often: from a faulty charger, a coin or a paper clip in the socket.
Try the charger in another car: maybe it’s the charger that’s broken.
Shine a light into the socket: is there any debris or a coin?
Check the fuse (below). On many cars it also powers the radio.
If it blows again, don’t fit a higher rating: there is a short in the socket.
In a 24 V system the cigarette lighter socket is often 24 V too. A 12 V charger may burn out — check the label on the charger.
The light means the engine control unit has stored a fault. You can’t find the cause without a scanner: it could be a cheap sensor or a serious failure.
If the light is flashing and the engine is misfiring, reduce the load and don’t drive far — you can ruin the catalytic converter.
If it’s on steadily and the car drives as usual, you can calmly drive to a workshop.
If you have an error code, decode it on the “Error codes” tab.

How an error code is structured
Cars and light trucks (OBD-II).

A code made of a letter and four characters, for example P0301. The letter is the system: P — engine and transmission, C — chassis (ABS, ESP), B — body (airbags, climate, lights), U — communication between control units. The digit after the letter: 0 and 2 — a generic code, the same for all makes; 1 — a manufacturer code.
Trucks and buses (J1939).

A code made of two numbers: SPN — which parameter or sensor, FMI — what is wrong with it (above normal, open circuit, short, etc.). For example, SPN 110 FMI 0 means engine coolant temperature above normal.
Some engines (Cummins on KAMAZ, MAN, Volvo) also show their own fault numbers. If the code is in a different format, send it to Oleg.
Motorcycles.

New motorcycles (Euro 5) have OBD-II codes, like cars. Many Japanese motorcycles show their own code as a number on the dash or by flashing the FI light: on Honda long flashes are tens, short ones are units. Oleg can add such codes to the reference for your make.
Write down the codes before clearing them. Clearing a code doesn’t mean fixing it: if the cause is still there, it will come back.

If the starter is silent or only clicks, most often the kill switch clip isn’t in place, the throttle lever isn’t in neutral or the battery is flat.
Check the kill switch clip on the lanyard: it must be in place in the switch on the remote control or the motor.
Put the throttle and shift lever in neutral: the motor won’t start in gear.
Check the battery terminals: water makes them corrode. Clean and tighten them.
Measure the battery: below 12.4 V — charge it.

The relay clicks but the starter doesn’t crank — check the heavy cable on the starter and the ground.
Flat battery? Many electric-start motors can be started with the emergency starter rope. It comes with the motor and is wound around the flywheel under the cowling. See the motor’s manual for how.
Fuel isn’t reaching the motor
If the bulb stays soft, fuel isn’t flowing: the tank vent is closed, the hose connector isn’t clicked in, or air is getting in.
Open the air vent on the fuel tank cap — otherwise fuel won’t flow.
Check the fuel hose connectors on the tank and the motor: push them in until they click.
Squeeze the bulb (arrow toward the motor) until it gets firm.
The bulb never gets firm — the hose is cracked or the bulb’s valves have failed. Replace the bulb.
Old fuel or fuel with water — drain it and fill with fresh. For a two-stroke motor, mix in oil at the right ratio.
Fuel is getting through: check the choke and spark plugs
A firm bulb means fuel is getting through. The motor usually won’t catch because of the choke or flooded or fouled spark plugs.
Cold carburetted motor: pull out the choke, start it and ease the choke back in.
If you’ve been pulling for a long time, the plugs may be flooded. Remove them, dry them, turn the motor over 5–6 times without plugs and refit them.
A plug that is black, sooty or wet with oil — replace it. On two-stroke motors plugs are replaced often.
Check the plug caps: pushed on until they click, no cracks.
Is the kill switch clip in place? Without it there’s no spark, even if the motor turns over.

No telltale water stream — shut the motor off
A stream of water should always come out of the hole on the side of the motor. No stream means water isn’t cooling the motor, and it can overheat within minutes.
Never run the motor without water, even on shore: the water pump impeller will burn out in seconds.
Shut the motor off.
Clear the telltale hole with a thin wire — it often clogs with sand.
Inspect the water intake on the motor’s lower unit: remove weeds, plastic bags, silt.
Start it again. Still no stream — the water pump impeller is most likely worn. It is replaced every 1–2 seasons.
If the motor beeps or the overheat light is on, don’t keep going until it’s repaired.
